slides.title: The E-Nose
slides.alt: The E-Nose and the 24 people it tested, 17 ticks and 7 crosses

setup.preamble: Joy can smell Parkinson's disease. Researchers at Zhejiang University built an AI-powered E-Nose to do the same, so the test could be used worldwide.
setup.para: They tested the E-Nose on $24$ people, $12$ with Parkinson's and $12$ without. It guessed $17$ of the $24$ correctly, so $\hat p=\tfrac{17}{24}\approx 0.708$. A machine that only guesses would be right with probability $p=0.5$ on each person.

facts.html: $\hat p=\tfrac{17}{24}\approx 0.708$: correct in the real test
$p=0.5$: the rate of a machine that only guesses

scene.alt: The E-Nose and the 24 people it tested, each guess a tick or a cross, beside a graph of sample proportions

slides.title: A machine that only guesses
slides.stem: In a world where the E-Nose only guesses, what would you expect $\hat p$ to be?

walk.cap: Each guess is right half the time
walk.note: Chance moves the count up or down from one test to the next, so it is not exactly $0.5$ every time.

scene.alt: The E-Nose and the 24 people it tested, each guess a tick or a cross, beside a graph of sample proportions

slides.title: Simulate a guessing machine
slides.stem: Each dot is one simulated test of a guessing machine: its $\hat p$. In $200$ tests, how often is $\hat p\ge 0.708$?

walk.cap: Count the dots at or beyond the dashed line
walk.note: A guessing machine rarely does this well, so $17$ correct would be surprising if the E-Nose only guessed.

scene.alt: The E-Nose and the 24 people it tested, each guess a tick or a cross, beside a graph of sample proportions

slides.title: The normal model for p̂
slides.stem: The dots pile up in a symmetric mound. Find the mean and standard deviation of the normal model for $\hat p$.

walk.note: The curve sits on the pile of simulated tests.

scene.alt: The E-Nose and the 24 people it tested, each guess a tick or a cross, beside a graph of sample proportions

slides.title: Luck, or a real nose?
slides.stem: Use the normal model. How likely is $\hat p\ge 0.708$ for a machine that only guesses?

walk.note: Only about a $2.1\%$ chance by luck alone, close to the $2.0\%$ of the simulations. We are convinced the E-Nose does better than guessing.

scene.alt: The E-Nose and the 24 people it tested, each guess a tick or a cross, beside a graph of sample proportions

slides.title: Ten times the people (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Now $n=240$ people and $170$ correct: still $\hat p=0.708$. Is a guessing machine more or less likely to reach it?

scene.alt: The E-Nose and the 24 people it tested, each guess a tick or a cross, beside a graph of sample proportions

slides.title: Ten times the people (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Now $n=240$ people and $170$ correct: still $\hat p=0.708$. Is a guessing machine more or less likely to reach it?

walk.note: Larger $n$, narrower curve: $0.708$ is now almost impossible by luck.

scene.alt: The E-Nose and the 24 people it tested, each guess a tick or a cross, beside a graph of sample proportions
